As a rule, this kind of rationalism therefore appeals, more or less openly, to the idea of a “divine” reason.
Reflective rationalism has to divide human reason in two.
First there is the reason that produces various coherent discourses. This is the reason presupposed by naive rationalism and rightly criticized by skepticism.

Then there is, so to speak, a higher reason—the Vernunft that German philosophy contrasts with Verstand. This higher reason reflects, hence my term “reflective rationalism,” on the discourses produced by the first reason and distinguishes those that are true, or evident, from those that are false or “doubtful.”
Every human being has his own “first” reason, since something that convinces me does not necessarily convince someone else.
But the higher reason is the same in everyone, since what is genuinely evident is evident to everyone.
It is therefore perfectly natural to regard this higher reason as standing above humanity—that is, as “divine,” eternal, and so on.
This divine reason possesses the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Human reason, by contrast, makes mistakes and knows truth only by participating in divine reason.
Divine reason creates reality. Human reason, by participating in divine reason, can therefore know reality before experience—that is, a priori.
Critical reason, incidentally, already operates with two forms of reason: one produces the various discourses, while the other identifies what they have in common.
In that case, however, the “divine” character of the second reason is less obvious.

“valid in another system” means “this is how it appears to someone else.”
“Secondary” qualities are those that change when the coordinates change. “Primary” qualities are those that remain identical despite the change.
But the weakness of this method appears immediately.
Physics does not in fact use every possible change of coordinates. It uses only particular kinds of transformations.
The definition of which qualities count as “primary” is therefore arbitrary.

And if we decided that only qualities remaining unchanged under every conceivable transformation could count as primary, the result would not merely be an extraordinary impoverishment of reality. It would be its complete annihilation.

Plato, however, denied that this omniscience could ever be attained. From his point of view, “dogmatics” must therefore always be submitted, again and again, to dialectical treatment. In this sense he can be regarded as the father of “liberalism,” although his political philosophy is far removed from the absurd bourgeois fairy tales of liberalism, since he believed that the State must exercise very strict control over “dialectic.”

In any case, Plato draws a very clear distinction between dialectic and dogmatics. In his dialogues he never gives an explicit answer to the problem under discussion: thesis and antithesis remain without a synthesis. Yet the answer—the synthesis—is contained within them, and the reader must work it out personally from the dialectical process that has been presented.
This emphasizes that the answer, meaning the synthesis or knowledge, lies outside dialectic. It already belongs to “dogmatics,” which Plato himself presented in his lost work On the Good.

It is easy to see that Plato’s dialectical method is analogous to the method used by physics, especially modern physics. By varying the coordinate system, physics rejects whatever is “valid” only within one particular system. Whatever remains unchanged under all these changes is regarded as true—that is, as corresponding to reality.

Dialectic does the same thing. It rejects whatever is “valid” only from the standpoint of one possible opinion. It treats as knowledge only what remains after this purification: what is valid from the standpoint of all possible opinions.
“Knowledge,” therefore, is nothing other than the invariant of “opinions.”

97) This is especially easy to see in Plotinus, who regarded himself as Plato’s successor but clearly failed to understand what Platonic dialectic was. See the Enneads, where dialectic is described as contemplation (I.3), and again where “contemplation” is treated as the fundamental method of philosophy and even as the supreme purpose of life as such (III.8).

At the beginning of Christian philosophy, however, we see the idea of dialectic revived, especially in Augustine. Later, at the beginning of modern bourgeois philosophy, Descartes revived it again, just as Hegel would revive it at the beginning of socialist philosophy.
Augustine knows that truth can be reached only through dialogue. But he does not speak with another human being; he speaks with God.

In one sense, this is a step backward. It obscures the social character of dialectic and indirectly prepares the way for Descartes’s solitary dialectic, which Descartes inherits from Augustine after dismissing God.

But in another sense it is a step forward. Augustine’s interaction with God does not consist only in discourse. It also contains elements beyond discourse and beyond reason: faith, love, prayer, ritual, the life of the righteous, and so on.

This indirectly prepares the way for Hegel’s correct understanding of dialectic as an active process. In Hegel, God is once again replaced by humanity—but not by isolated, accidental individuals, as in Plato. He is replaced by humanity in the full course of its historical development.
In one sense, Plato and Augustine are merely the thesis and antithesis from which the Hegelian synthesis emerges:
human–discourse, God–action, human–action; isolated individual, universal God, universal humanity.
